blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Rest:

If position of particle does not change with time with respect to reference then it is at rest.

Motion:

If position of particle changes with time with respect to reference then it is called in motion.

Frame of Reference:

It is the reference with respect to which position or motion of particle is defined. Motion and Rest are relative terms which depends on Frame of reference.

Types of Motion :

(A)1-D Motion: If position changes with time  along a straight line with respect to frame of reference. Example: Motion of Train Along Straight Track etc.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 (B)2-D Motion: If position changes in a plane with time with respect to frame of reference . Examples: Projectile Motion, Circular Motion etc.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 (C)3-D Motion: If position changes in space with time with respect to frame of reference. Examples: Motions of Kite etc.

Position Vector : It is used to specify the position of a certain particle.

Direction: Always points from the Reference point (origin) to a given point.

Position Vector $\vec{r}=X \hat{\imath}+Y\hat{\jmath}+Z \hat{k}$

Distance: Actual length of the path traversed by the particle between initial and final position is called distance.

It is a Scalar Quantity.

S.I.→ Metre (m)

C.G.S.→ Centimetre (cm)

Distance cannot be negative.

Displacement: Shortest distance between initial & final position of the particle is called displacement.

Displacement is a vector quantity, and its direction is always from initial position to final position.

Displacement does not depend on path followed by particle. It depends only on initial & final position of the particle.

Displacement in Vector Form

$\vec{r}_1=x_1 \hat{i}+y_1 \hat{j}+z_1 \hat{k}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_2=\mathrm{x}_2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\mathrm{y}_2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\mathrm{z}_2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$

$\text { Displacement vector } \Delta \overrightarrow{\mathbf{r}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_2-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_1$

$\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}=\left(\mathrm{x}_2-\mathrm{x}_1\right) \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\left(\mathrm{y}_2-\mathrm{y}_1\right) \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\left(\mathrm{z}_2-\mathrm{z}_1\right) \hat{\mathrm{k}}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
A particle starts from point A (1, –1, 0) m and reaches at point B (5, 3, –2) m, reference point is origin. Find:

(1) Initial position vector

(2) Final position vector

(3) Displacement vector

(4) Length of shortest path
blocks.answer:
(1) Initial position vector  $\mathbf{OA} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$

(2) Final position vector  $\mathbf{OB} = 5\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$

(3) Displacement = $\left( \mathbf{OB} - \mathbf{OA} \right) = (5 - 1)\hat{i} + (3 + 1)\hat{j} + (-2 - 0)\hat{k}$ =$4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$

(4) Magnitude of Displacement = $\sqrt{4^2 + 4^2 + 2^2}$  = 6m

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Speed - The Rate at which distance is covered with respect to time is called speed.

It is a Scalar quantity.

S.I unit- m/s,

Dimension- $M^0 L^1 T^{-1}$

Types of speed :-                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             1. Uniform speed- Particle covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.                                                                                                                                                      2. Non-uniform Speed (Variable Speed)-Particle covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time.                                                                                                         3. Average Speed - When a particle is moving with variable speed then

Case 1: For a given time interval it is defined as ratio of total distance travelled to total time taken.

$V_{a v g}=\frac{\text { Total Distance covered }}{\text { Total time }}=\frac{s_1+s_2+s_3+\ldots . .+s_n}{t_1+t_2+t_3+\ldots \ldots .+t_n}=\frac{v_1 t_1+v_2 t_2+v_3 t_3+\ldots . .}{t_1+t_2+t_3+\ldots \ldots .}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { If } \mathrm{t}_1=\mathrm{t}_2=\mathrm{t}_3=\ldots \ldots . . .=\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm{n}} \text { then } \\ & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{v}_2+\ldots \ldots \ldots . .+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\mathrm{n}} \end{aligned}$

For 2 equal intervals of times:

$V_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{v}_2}{2}$

Case 2 :If a person moves a certain distance in n equal parts with different speeds.

$V_{\text {avg }}=\frac{d}{\frac{d}{n v_1}+\frac{d}{n v_2}+\ldots . . \frac{d}{n v_n}}$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_2}+\ldots \ldots \ldots \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}}}$

For 2 equal distances:

$V_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1+v_2}$

Graphically, it is equal to the slope of a straight line  joining two points on the distance-time graph.

4. Instantaneous speed- It is the speed of a particle at a particular instant of time.

$v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$

Graphically, it is equal to the slope of the tangent at any point on the distance-time graph.

Velocity - The rate of change of position with time is called velocity.

It is a Vector quantity

S.I unit- $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$,

Dimension - $M^0 L^1 T^{-1}$

Types of Velocity:

1. Uniform velocity - If magnitude as well as direction of velocity of particle remains same.

2. Non-uniform velocity (Variable velocity )- If either magnitude or direction or both varies.

3. Average velocity - When particle is moving with variable velocity then,

$\text { Average velocity }=\dfrac{\text { Net Displacement }}{\text { Time taken }} \Rightarrow \vec{V}_{\text {avg }}=\dfrac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{\vec{r}_f-\vec{r}_i}{t_f-t_i}$

Graphically it is equal to the slope of straight line joining two points on displacement-time graph.

Time Average Velocity =$\text { If } v=f(t) \Rightarrow\langle v\rangle=\dfrac{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v d t}{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} d t}$

Space Average Velocity=$\text { If } v=f(x) \Rightarrow\langle v\rangle=\dfrac{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} v d x}{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} d x}$

4. Instantaneous velocity - It is the velocity of a particle at a particular instant of time.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\text {inst }}=\lim _{\Delta \mathrm{t} \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}\right) \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\text {inst }}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

Graphically it is equal to the slope of tangent at any point on displacement-time graph.

Change in velocity:

$\begin{aligned} &\Delta \vec{v}=\vec{v}_f-\vec{v}_i\\ &\text { If }\left|\vec{v}_{\mathrm{f}}\right|=\left|\vec{v}_i\right|=v \text {, then } \end{aligned}$

$|\Delta \vec{v}|=2 \mathrm{v} \sin \left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$

where $\theta$ is the angle between initial and final velocity

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A bird flies due north at velocity 20 m/s for 15 s it rests for 5 s and then flies due south at velocity 24m/s for 10 s. For the whole trip find the average speed and magnitude of average velocity.
blocks.answer:
Solution

$\displaystyle \text{Average Speed} = \frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}} = \frac{20 \times 15 + 24 \times 10}{15+5+10} = \frac{540}{30} = 18 \, \text{m/s}$

$\displaystyle\text{Average Velocity} = \frac{\text{Displacement}}{\text{Total Time}} = \frac{(20 \times 15) \hat{j}+(24 \times 10)(-\hat{j})}{15+5+10}= \frac{60\hat{j}}{30} = 2\hat{j}$

$\text{Magnitude of Average Velocity} = |2\hat{j}| = 2 \, \text{m/s}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Acceleration -  Rate of change in velocity with respect to time.

It is a Vector quantity.

S.I unit- $\dfrac{m}{s^2}$,

Dimension- $M^0 L^1 T^{-2}$

There are 3 ways to change a velocity (vector)

1. Only magnitude change

2.Only direction change

3.Both direction and magnitude changes

Types of Acceleration

1. Uniform Acceleration - If the magnitude and direction of the acceleration remain constant during the motion

2. Non-uniform Acceleration (Variable Acceleration)-If either magnitude or direction or both change during motion.

3. Average Acceleration - It is the ratio of total change in velocity to the total time taken by the particle

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\dfrac{\text { change in velocity }}{\text { time interval }}=\dfrac{\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{f}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$

Direction of average acceleration is along the change in velocity

Graphically it is equal to the slope of straight line joining two points on velocity-time graph.

4. Instantaneous Acceleration - It is the acceleration of a particle at a particular instant of time.

$\vec{a}_{\text {inst }}=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\Delta v}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{a}_{\text {inst }}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dv}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad \text { When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { in function of time }(\mathrm{t}) .$

i.e. first derivative of velocity is called instantaneous acceleration

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{dt}^2} \quad\left[\mathrm{As} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right]$

i.e. second derivative of position vector is called instantaneous acceleration

$\vec{a}_{\text {inst }}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dv}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dx}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {inst }}=\mathrm{v} \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dx}} \quad \text { When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { in function of position }(\mathrm{x}) \text {. }$

Application of Calculus

$\text { For } \mathrm{v}-\mathrm{t} \text { relation } \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

$\text { For } \mathrm{v}-\mathrm{x} \text { relation } \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{v} \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dx}}$

Key points:

  • When particle moves with constant velocity then its acceleration will be zero. If particle moves with constant velocity then
$v_{\mathrm{avg}}=\left|\vec{v}_{\mathrm{avg}}\right|=v_{\text {inst }}=\left|\vec{v}_{\text {inst }}\right|$

  • Acceleration which opposes the motion of body is called retardation. Increment or decrement in speed depends on direction of  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { and } \vec{a} \text {. }$
If $ \vec{v} \text { and } \vec{a} $ are in same direction then speed increases .

If $ \vec{v} \text { and } \vec{a} $ are in opposite direction then speed decreases.

Angle between  $ \vec{v}~ \& ~\vec{a} \text { is } 90^{\circ} $ or they are orthogonal, speed remains constant

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• When particle moves with constant velocity then magnitude of displacement and distance covered by particle is same.
  • A particle may have constant speed but variable velocity.
  • Example: When a particle is performing, Uniform circular motion then, for every instant of its circular motion, its speed remains constant, but velocity changes at every instant.
  • When a particle is moving on any path, the magnitude of instantaneous velocity is equal to the instantaneous speed.
  • When velocity is constant then motion is said to be uniform.

blocks.question:

(ii) Position of a particle is given by  $x = (6t^2 - t^3) \, \text{m}$, then find out its position when velocity becomes maximum.
blocks.answer:
Solution

(i) $\displaystyle \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}} \implies v \frac{d v}{d x}=\sqrt{x+1} \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x+1}}=\frac{1}{2}$

(ii) $x = 6t^2 - t^3 \implies v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 12t - 3t^2 \\[10 pt]  \text{For maximum velocity:} \quad \frac{dv}{dt} = 0 \implies 12 - 6t = 0 \implies t = 2 \text{ sec}  \\[10 pt] \therefore \quad \text{Position at } t = 2 \text{ sec.} \quad \\[10 pt] x = 6(2)^2 - (2)^3 = 16 \text{ m}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Motion under Gravity -Acceleration produced in the body by the force of gravity, is called acceleration due to gravity. It is represented by the symbol g.In the absence of air, it is found that all bodies (irrespective of the size, weight or composition) fall with the same acceleration near the surface of the earth. This motion of a body falling towards the earth from a small altitude (h << earth's radius) is called motion under gravity. Free fall means acceleration of body is equal to acceleration due to gravity.

Negative and positive sign are matter of our choice, so we can select any direction as positive and opposite side as negative.

(A) Vertical Projection from ground :

Equations of motion - Taking initial position as origin and direction of motion (i.e. vertically up) as positive and (vertical downward) as negative.

u (initial velocity) = +u

a (acceleration) = –g

at time t, Final velocity = v

height above ground = h

$ v = u - gt $ .................(1)

$h = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.............(2)

$v^2=u^2-2 g h$...........(3)

$h_{n^{th}} = u - \frac{g}{2} (2n - 1)
$

Maximum height (H)  $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$

Total time of flight(T)  $T = \dfrac{2u}{g}$

(B) Body dropped from some height :

Equations of Motion :

Taking initial position as origin and direction of motion (i.e., downward direction) as a positive, here we have

u = 0 [As body starts from rest]

a = +g [As acceleration is in the direction of motion]

at time t, final velocity = v

height below dropping point = h

v = gt ............(1)

h= $\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$........(2)

$v^2=2 g h$ ............(3)

Time to reach bottom(T)    $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$

Maximum speed (at bottom) $v^2 = 2gh$

$\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{gh}}$

Effect of Air Resistance :

Case-1 For ascending motion :

Time to go up,

$t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g+a}}$

Velocity of projection,

$v_1 = \sqrt{2h(g+a)}$

Case-2 For descending motion (downward motion) :

Time to go up [By assuming air resistance to be constant and considerable]

$t_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g-a}}$

Velocity on reaching ground

$v_2 = \sqrt{2h(g-a)}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
A ball is projected vertically upward with a speed of 50 m/s. Find :

(a) the maximum height

(b) the time to reach the maximum height

(c) the speed at half the maximum height

(d) time of flight

(e) velocity after t = 1 and t = 6 s

(f) height from ground at t = 1 and t = 5 sec
blocks.answer:
Solution

(a)  Initial velocity of ball (u)=50m/s, acceleration of ball =−g,

final velocity at the highest point (v)=0

So applying the 3rd equation of motion we get:

$\mathrm{v}^2=\mathrm{u}^2-2 \mathrm{gh}_{\operatorname{max}}$

$\Rightarrow 0=50^2-2 \times 10 \times \mathrm{h}_{\max } $

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{h}_{\max }=\frac{2500}{20}=125 \mathrm{~m}$

(b) Let the time required to reach max height be t. Then applying 1st equation of motion we get:

v = u − gt

0 = 50 − 10t

t = 5s

(c) Let speed at half of max height be V then:

$v^2=50^2-2 \mathrm{~g} \frac{125}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{~v}^2=2500-1250=1250 $

$\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{1250}=35.35 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

(d)  $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \mathrm{u}}{\mathrm{~g}}=\frac{50 \times 2}{10}=10 \mathrm{sec}$

(e) velocity after one second

v = u – gt

v = 50 – 10 × 1 = 40 m/s

velocity after 6 sec

v = 50 – 10 × 6 = –10m/s or 10ms downward

(f) Height after one second from ground

$h = 50 - \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10$

h=45m

height after 6 sec from ground

$h = 50 \times 6- \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10\times 36$

h = 120m

blocks.text:
Slope of a-t graph defines nothing

But Area of a-t graph gives change in velocity

$\text { Area of a-t graph }=\int \mathrm{adt}=\int \mathrm{dv}=\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1=\text { change in velocity }$

$\text { Area } \neq \text { final velocity }$

Graphs-1 - Uniform or constant acceleration

Graphs-2 -Uniformly increasing acceleration

Case-I

Explanation: In practice, at any instant body can not have two velocities or displacements or accelerations simultaneously.

Case-II

Explanation: Speed or distance can never be negative.

Case-III

Explanation : It is not possible to change any quantity without consuming time i.e. time can't be constant.

Graphical Problems in Horizontal Motion

If a car, starts from rest moves with constant acceleration $\alpha$ for some time retards uniformly at rate $\beta$ and finally comes at rest total time of motion is T

$\mathrm{v}_{\max }=\left(\dfrac{\alpha \beta}{\alpha+\beta}\right) \mathrm{T}$

$\mathrm{s}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\alpha \beta}{\alpha+\beta}\right) \mathrm{T}^2$

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
As $h=(1 / 2) g t^2$ , i.e., $ h \propto t^2$ , distance covered in time t, 2t, 3t , etc., will be in the ratio of $1^2: 2^2: 3^2$, i.e., square of consecutive integers. (in case of free fall, from rest)

A particle at rest, is dropped vertically from a height. The time taken by it to fall through successive distance of 1m each will then be in the ratio of the difference in the square roots of the integers i.e. $\sqrt{1},(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1}),(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}),(\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{3}), \ldots .$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Projectile Motion: When a body moves with constant acceleration such that its initial velocity and acceleration are non- collinear then its path is parabola and motion is known as projectile motion.

Projectile Motion = Horizontal Motion + Vertical Motion

$\begin{aligned} & u_x=u \cos \theta ; u_y=u \sin \theta \\ & a_x=0 \quad a_y=-g \\ & v_x=u_x=u \cos \theta v_y=u_y-g t \\ & x=(u \cos \theta) t \\ & y=(u \sin \theta) t-\frac{1}{2} g t^2 \end{aligned}$

Horizontal Motion

• Initial velocity in horizontal direction $=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}$

  • Acceleration along horizontal direction $=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{x}}=0 . \text { (Neglect air resistance) }$
  • Therefore, Horizontal velocity remains unchanged.
  • At any instant horizontal velocity $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta$
  • In time t, displacement along horizontal direction or x co-ordinate is, $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{t} \text { or } \mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta) \mathrm{t}$
Vertical Motion

• It is motion under the effect of gravity so that as particle moves upwards the magnitude of its vertical velocity decreases.

• Initial velocity in vertical direction $=u \sin \theta=u_y$

  • Acceleration along vertical direction $=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{y}}=-\mathrm{g}(\text { Neglect air resistance })$
  • At any instant, vertical speed $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}-\mathrm{gt}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta-\mathrm{gt}$
  • In time t, displacement in vertical direction or "height" of the particle above the ground $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}} \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2$
  • Equations of motion should be applied separately for x and y directions.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Projectile motion = Horizontal motion + Vertical motion

$\begin{array}{rl} \text { Horizontal } {\text { motion }} & \text { Vertical motion } \\ u_x=u & u_y=0 \\ a_x=0 & a_y=-g \\ v_x=u_x=u & v_y=-g t \\ \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{ut} & \mathrm{y}= - \frac{g t^2}{2} \end{array}$

Equation of Trajectory : $\quad \mathrm{y}=-\frac{g x^2}{2 u^2}$

Velocity at a General Point : $v=\sqrt{u^2+g^2 t^2}$

$\tan \theta=\frac{v_y}{v_x}$

$\tan \theta=-\frac{\mathrm{gt}}{\mathrm{u}}$

Time of Flight : $\quad T=\sqrt{\frac{2 H}{g}}$

Horizontal Range : $\quad R=u \sqrt{\frac{2 H}{g}}$

CASE 1: Projection from a height at an angle θ above horizontal:

$\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta \quad \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta$

$\mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta) \mathrm{t} \quad \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{y}}=- \mathrm{g}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{H}=(\mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2 \end{aligned}$

Case 2 : Projection from a height at an angle θ Below horizontal:

$\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta \quad \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta$

$\mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta) \mathrm{t} \quad \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{g}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{H}=(\mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{2} g \mathrm{t}^2 \\ & \mathrm{gt}^2+(2 \mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{t}-2 \mathrm{H}=0 \end{aligned}$

Velocity after falling height h

$v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}=\sqrt{u^2+2 g h}$

Note: Four objects are projected with same speed ‘u’ from top of a tower of height ‘h’ then their speed when they reach the ground is $v=\sqrt{u^2+2 g h}$

$v \text { is independent of } \theta$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Concept of Relative Motion

Relative Displacement:

Displacement of B with respect to A = Displacement of B as measured from A

$\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{BA}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{A}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{BA}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{dt}}-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{BA}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{A}}$

Relative = Actual – Reference

For same direction : When two particles are moving in the same direction, then magnitude of their relative velocity is equal to the difference between their individual speeds.

$\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{12}\right| \text { or }\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{21}\right|=\mathrm{v}_1 \sim \mathrm{v}_2$ ( Positive Difference )

For opposite directions : When two particles are moving in the opposite directions, then magnitude of their relative velocity is always equal to the sum of their individual speeds.

$\left|\vec{v}_{12}\right| \text { or }\left|\vec{v}_{21}\right|=v_1+v_2$

Note:- When two particles move simultaneously then the concept of relative motion becomes applicable conveniently.

Numerical Applications

(1) When two particles are moving along a straight line with constant speeds then their relative acceleration must be zero and, in this condition, relative velocity is the ratio of relative displacement to time.

$\displaystyle$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}_1=\text { const. } \quad \mathrm{v}_2=\text { const. } \\ & \text { when } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {rel. }}=0 \\ & \mathrm{v}_{\text {rel. }}=\dfrac{\mathrm{s}_{\text {Relative }}}{\text { time }} \end{aligned}$$

(2) When two particles move in such a way that their relative acceleration non-zero but constant then we apply equations of motion in the relative form.

$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{AB}} & =\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{A}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{B}} \\ & =0-\mathrm{a}=-\mathrm{a} \neq 0=\text { constant } \end{aligned}$

Equations of Motion (Relative)

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{rel}}+\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{rel}} \mathrm{t} \\ & \mathrm{~s}_{\text {rel. }}=\mathrm{u}_{\text {rel. }} \mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{a}_{\text {rel. }} \mathrm{t}^2 \\ & v_{\text {rel. }}^2=u_{\text {rel. }}^2+2 \cdot a_{\text {rel. }} s_{\text {rel. }} \\ & \mathrm{s}_{\mathrm{rel} .}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{rel} .}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel} .}\right) \mathrm{t} \end{aligned}$

Relative velocity in a plane

Relative velocity of A with respect to 'B' can be calculated as

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{v}_{A B}=\vec{v}_A-\vec{v}_B \\ & \left|\vec{v}_{A B}\right|=\sqrt{v_A^2+v_B^2-2 v_A \cdot v_B \cos \theta} \end{aligned}$

Note:

For two particles to collide:

(1) Their combined relative displacement becomes zero.

(2) Their combined vertical velocities will be same: if they are projected from same level at the same time (in case of projectiles)

(3) Their combined motion can be converted into two 1D motions.

Relative path of a projectiles w.r.t. another projectile

Two projectiles are thrown from ground with different velocities at different angles. Since both projectiles have equal accelerations so their relative acceleration is zero. Thus, path of one projectile w.r.t. other is a straight line and motion of one projectile w.r.t. other is uniform.

$\text { If } u_1 \cos \theta_1=u_2 \cos \theta_2 \text { then relative path is a vertical line. }$

$\text { If } u_1 \sin \theta_1=u_2 \sin \theta_2 \text { then relative path is a horizontal line. }$

blocks.question: Buses A and B are moving in the same direction with speeds 20 m/s and 15 m/s respectively. Find the relative velocity of A w.r.t. B and relative velocity of B w.r.t A.
blocks.answer:
$\text { Let their direction of motion be along }+\mathrm{x} \text {-axis then } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_A=(20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}) \mathrm{\hat i} \text { and } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{B}}=(15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}) \mathrm{\hat i}$

i.e. A is moving with speed 5 m/s w.r.t B in the same direction.

$\begin{aligned} &\text { (b) Relative velocity of B w.r.t. } \left.\left.A \text { is } \vec{v}_{\mathrm{BA}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{A}}=\text { (actual velocity of } \mathrm{B}\right)- \text { (velocity of } \mathrm{A}\right)\\ &=(15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathrm{i}}-(20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathrm{i}}=(-5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathrm{i}}=(5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})(-\hat{\mathrm{i}}) \end{aligned}$

i.e. B is moving in opposite direction w.r.t. A, at a speed 5 m/s

blocks.question: Three boys A, B and C are situated at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side d at t = 0. Each of the boys move with constant speed v. A always moves towards B, B towards C and C towards A. when and where will they meet each other?
blocks.answer:
By symmetry they will meet at the centroid of the triangle. Approaching velocity of A and B towards each other is v + v cos 60° and they cover distance d when they meet.So that time taken, is given by

$\therefore t=\dfrac{d}{v+v \cos 60^{\circ}}=\dfrac{d}{v+\dfrac{v}{2}}=\dfrac{2 d}{3 v}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Misunderstanding Frames of Reference: Not clearly defining the observer's frame of reference can lead to confusion.

2. Incorrect Vector Addition: Failing to properly add or subtract velocity vectors, especially when directions differ.

3. Ignoring the Effect of Motion of the Observer: Forgetting that the observer's motion affects perceived speeds.

4. Neglecting Direction: Ignoring the importance of direction in relative velocity calculations.

5. Confusing Relative Speed and Actual Speed: Misinterpreting relative speed as the actual speed of an object

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Rain-Man Concept

(1) If rain is falling vertically with a velocity $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$ and an observer is moving horizontally with speed  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}$ then the velocity of rain relative to observer will be

$\vec{v}_{R M}=\vec{v}_R-\vec{v}_M \Rightarrow \vec{v}_{R M}=-\vec{v}_R \hat{j}-\vec{v}_M \hat{i}$

$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}^2}$

The direction of  $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}$ is such that it makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical given by $\theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}} / \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}\right)$

$$(2) If rain is already falling at an angle $\theta$ with the vertical with a velocity $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$ and an observer is moving horizontally with speed $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}$ finds that the rain drops are hitting on his head vertically downwards

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Here } \vec{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}\\ &\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \sin \theta-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}\right) \mathrm{\hat i}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \cos \theta \hat{\mathrm{j}} \end{aligned}$

For rain to appear falling vertically, the horizontal component of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{RM}}$ should be zero.

{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}} \sin \theta-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}=0 \Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}}$

$\text { and }\left|\vec{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}\right|=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \cos \theta=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \sqrt{1-\sin ^2 \theta}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \sqrt{1-\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}^2}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}^2}$

River-Boat (or Man) Problem

A man can swim with velocity $\vec{v}$, i.e. it is the velocity of man w.r.t. still water.

If water is also flowing with velocity $\vec{v}_R$ then velocity of man relative to ground $ \vec{v}_m=\vec{v}+\vec{v}_R$

Case(1) If the swimming is in the direction of flow of water or along the downstream then  $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}$

Case(2) If the swimming is in the direction opposite to the flow of water or along the upstream then $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}$

Case(3) If the man is crossing the river i.e. $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$ are non colinear then use vector algebra. $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{m}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$

For shortest path :If a man wants to cross the river such that his "displacement should be minimum".

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{m}}=\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}\right)$It is in the direction of displacement AB.

$\text { To reach at } B $,  $\mathrm v \sin \theta=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mathrm{v}}$

$\text { Time taken } \mathrm{T}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{v} \cos \theta}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{v}^2-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2}}$

For minimum time:  To cross the river in minimum time, the velocity along AB $(v \cos \theta)$ should be maximum.

It is possible if $\theta=0$  i.e. swimming should start perpendicular to water current.

$\text { Minimum time }=\mathrm{t}_{\min }=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{v}}$

In time $\mathrm{t}_{\text {min }}$swimmer travels distance  BC along the river with speed of river  $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \therefore \mathrm{BC}=\mathbf{t}_{\min } \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{R}}$

$\text { Distance travelled along river flow }=\text { drift of } \operatorname{man}=t_{\min } v_R=\dfrac{d}{V} v_R$

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• When particle moves with constant velocity then magnitude of displacement and distance covered by particle is same.
  • A particle may have constant speed but variable velocity.
  • Example: When a particle is performing, Uniform circular motion then, for every instant of its circular motion, its speed remains constant, but velocity changes at every instant.
  • When a particle is moving on any path, the magnitude of instantaneous velocity is equal to the instantaneous speed.
  • When velocity is constant then motion is said to be uniform.

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
As $h=(1 / 2) g t^2$ , i.e., $ h \propto t^2$ , distance covered in time t, 2t, 3t , etc., will be in the ratio of $1^2: 2^2: 3^2$, i.e., square of consecutive integers. (in case of free fall, from rest)

A particle at rest, is dropped vertically from a height. The time taken by it to fall through successive distance of 1m each will then be in the ratio of the difference in the square roots of the integers i.e. $\sqrt{1},(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1}),(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}),(\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{3}), \ldots .$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Speed - The Rate at which distance is covered with respect to time is called speed.

It is a Scalar quantity.

S.I unit- m/s,

Dimension- $M^0 L^1 T^{-1}$

Types of speed :-                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             1. Uniform speed- Particle covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.                                                                                                                                                      2. Non-uniform Speed (Variable Speed)-Particle covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time.                                                                                                         3. Average Speed - When a particle is moving with variable speed then

Case 1: For a given time interval it is defined as ratio of total distance travelled to total time taken.

$V_{a v g}=\frac{\text { Total Distance covered }}{\text { Total time }}=\frac{s_1+s_2+s_3+\ldots . .+s_n}{t_1+t_2+t_3+\ldots \ldots .+t_n}=\frac{v_1 t_1+v_2 t_2+v_3 t_3+\ldots . .}{t_1+t_2+t_3+\ldots \ldots .}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { If } \mathrm{t}_1=\mathrm{t}_2=\mathrm{t}_3=\ldots \ldots . . .=\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm{n}} \text { then } \\ & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{v}_2+\ldots \ldots \ldots . .+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\mathrm{n}} \end{aligned}$

For 2 equal intervals of times:

$V_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{v}_2}{2}$

Case 2 :If a person moves a certain distance in n equal parts with different speeds.

$V_{\text {avg }}=\frac{d}{\frac{d}{n v_1}+\frac{d}{n v_2}+\ldots . . \frac{d}{n v_n}}$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_2}+\ldots \ldots \ldots \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}}}$

For 2 equal distances:

$V_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1+v_2}$

Graphically, it is equal to the slope of a straight line  joining two points on the distance-time graph.

4. Instantaneous speed- It is the speed of a particle at a particular instant of time.

$v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$

Graphically, it is equal to the slope of the tangent at any point on the distance-time graph.

Velocity - The rate of change of position with time is called velocity.

It is a Vector quantity

S.I unit- $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$,

Dimension - $M^0 L^1 T^{-1}$

Types of Velocity:

1. Uniform velocity - If magnitude as well as direction of velocity of particle remains same.

2. Non-uniform velocity (Variable velocity )- If either magnitude or direction or both varies.

3. Average velocity - When particle is moving with variable velocity then,

$\text { Average velocity }=\dfrac{\text { Net Displacement }}{\text { Time taken }} \Rightarrow \vec{V}_{\text {avg }}=\dfrac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{\vec{r}_f-\vec{r}_i}{t_f-t_i}$

Graphically it is equal to the slope of straight line joining two points on displacement-time graph.

Time Average Velocity =$\text { If } v=f(t) \Rightarrow\langle v\rangle=\dfrac{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v d t}{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} d t}$

Space Average Velocity=$\text { If } v=f(x) \Rightarrow\langle v\rangle=\dfrac{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} v d x}{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} d x}$

4. Instantaneous velocity - It is the velocity of a particle at a particular instant of time.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\text {inst }}=\lim _{\Delta \mathrm{t} \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}\right) \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\text {inst }}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

Graphically it is equal to the slope of tangent at any point on displacement-time graph.

Change in velocity:

$\begin{aligned} &\Delta \vec{v}=\vec{v}_f-\vec{v}_i\\ &\text { If }\left|\vec{v}_{\mathrm{f}}\right|=\left|\vec{v}_i\right|=v \text {, then } \end{aligned}$

$|\Delta \vec{v}|=2 \mathrm{v} \sin \left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$

where $\theta$ is the angle between initial and final velocity

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Acceleration -  Rate of change in velocity with respect to time.

It is a Vector quantity.

S.I unit- $\dfrac{m}{s^2}$,

Dimension- $M^0 L^1 T^{-2}$

There are 3 ways to change a velocity (vector)

1. Only magnitude change

2.Only direction change

3.Both direction and magnitude changes

Types of Acceleration

1. Uniform Acceleration - If the magnitude and direction of the acceleration remain constant during the motion

2. Non-uniform Acceleration (Variable Acceleration)-If either magnitude or direction or both change during motion.

3. Average Acceleration - It is the ratio of total change in velocity to the total time taken by the particle

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\dfrac{\text { change in velocity }}{\text { time interval }}=\dfrac{\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{f}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$

Direction of average acceleration is along the change in velocity

Graphically it is equal to the slope of straight line joining two points on velocity-time graph.

4. Instantaneous Acceleration - It is the acceleration of a particle at a particular instant of time.

$\vec{a}_{\text {inst }}=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\Delta v}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \vec{a}_{\text {inst }}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dv}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad \text { When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { in function of time }(\mathrm{t}) .$

i.e. first derivative of velocity is called instantaneous acceleration

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{dt}^2} \quad\left[\mathrm{As} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right]$

i.e. second derivative of position vector is called instantaneous acceleration

$\vec{a}_{\text {inst }}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dv}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dx}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {inst }}=\mathrm{v} \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dx}} \quad \text { When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { in function of position }(\mathrm{x}) \text {. }$

Application of Calculus

$\text { For } \mathrm{v}-\mathrm{t} \text { relation } \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

$\text { For } \mathrm{v}-\mathrm{x} \text { relation } \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{v} \dfrac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dx}}$

Key points:

  • When particle moves with constant velocity then its acceleration will be zero. If particle moves with constant velocity then
$v_{\mathrm{avg}}=\left|\vec{v}_{\mathrm{avg}}\right|=v_{\text {inst }}=\left|\vec{v}_{\text {inst }}\right|$

  • Acceleration which opposes the motion of body is called retardation. Increment or decrement in speed depends on direction of  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { and } \vec{a} \text {. }$
If $ \vec{v} \text { and } \vec{a} $ are in same direction then speed increases .

If $ \vec{v} \text { and } \vec{a} $ are in opposite direction then speed decreases.

Angle between  $ \vec{v}~ \& ~\vec{a} \text { is } 90^{\circ} $ or they are orthogonal, speed remains constant

Area under the v-t curve gives

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Motion under Gravity -Acceleration produced in the body by the force of gravity, is called acceleration due to gravity. It is represented by the symbol g.In the absence of air, it is found that all bodies (irrespective of the size, weight or composition) fall with the same acceleration near the surface of the earth. This motion of a body falling towards the earth from a small altitude (h << earth's radius) is called motion under gravity. Free fall means acceleration of body is equal to acceleration due to gravity.

Negative and positive sign are matter of our choice, so we can select any direction as positive and opposite side as negative.

(A) Vertical Projection from ground :

Equations of motion - Taking initial position as origin and direction of motion (i.e. vertically up) as positive and (vertical downward) as negative.

u (initial velocity) = +u

a (acceleration) = –g

at time t, Final velocity = v

height above ground = h

$ v = u - gt $ .................(1)

$h = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.............(2)

$v^2=u^2-2 g h$...........(3)

$h_{n^{th}} = u - \frac{g}{2} (2n - 1)
$

Maximum height (H)  $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$

Total time of flight(T)  $T = \dfrac{2u}{g}$

(B) Body dropped from some height :

Equations of Motion :

Taking initial position as origin and direction of motion (i.e., downward direction) as a positive, here we have

u = 0 [As body starts from rest]

a = +g [As acceleration is in the direction of motion]

at time t, final velocity = v

height below dropping point = h

v = gt ............(1)

h= $\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$........(2)

$v^2=2 g h$ ............(3)

Time to reach bottom(T)    $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$

Maximum speed (at bottom) $v^2 = 2gh$

$\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{gh}}$

Effect of Air Resistance :

Case-1 For ascending motion :

Time to go up,

$t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g+a}}$

Velocity of projection,

$v_1 = \sqrt{2h(g+a)}$

Case-2 For descending motion (downward motion) :

Time to go up [By assuming air resistance to be constant and considerable]

Velocity on reaching ground

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Projectile Motion: When a body moves with constant acceleration such that its initial velocity and acceleration are non- collinear then its path is parabola and motion is known as projectile motion.

Projectile Motion = Horizontal Motion + Vertical Motion

$\begin{aligned} & u_x=u \cos \theta ; u_y=u \sin \theta \\ & a_x=0 \quad a_y=-g \\ & v_x=u_x=u \cos \theta v_y=u_y-g t \\ & x=(u \cos \theta) t \\ & y=(u \sin \theta) t-\frac{1}{2} g t^2 \end{aligned}$

Horizontal Motion

• Initial velocity in horizontal direction $=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}$

  • Acceleration along horizontal direction $=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{x}}=0 . \text { (Neglect air resistance) }$
  • Therefore, Horizontal velocity remains unchanged.
  • At any instant horizontal velocity $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta$
  • In time t, displacement along horizontal direction or x co-ordinate is, $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{t} \text { or } \mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta) \mathrm{t}$
Vertical Motion

• It is motion under the effect of gravity so that as particle moves upwards the magnitude of its vertical velocity decreases.

• Initial velocity in vertical direction $=u \sin \theta=u_y$

  • Acceleration along vertical direction $=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{y}}=-\mathrm{g}(\text { Neglect air resistance })$
  • At any instant, vertical speed $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}-\mathrm{gt}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta-\mathrm{gt}$
  • In time t, displacement in vertical direction or "height" of the particle above the ground $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}} \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2$
  • Equations of motion should be applied separately for x and y directions.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Projectile motion = Horizontal motion + Vertical motion

$\begin{array}{rl} \text { Horizontal } {\text { motion }} & \text { Vertical motion } \\ u_x=u & u_y=0 \\ a_x=0 & a_y=-g \\ v_x=u_x=u & v_y=-g t \\ \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{ut} & \mathrm{y}= - \frac{g t^2}{2} \end{array}$

Equation of Trajectory : $\quad \mathrm{y}=-\frac{g x^2}{2 u^2}$

Velocity at a General Point : $v=\sqrt{u^2+g^2 t^2}$

$\tan \theta=\frac{v_y}{v_x}$

$\tan \theta=-\frac{\mathrm{gt}}{\mathrm{u}}$

Time of Flight : $\quad T=\sqrt{\frac{2 H}{g}}$

Horizontal Range : $\quad R=u \sqrt{\frac{2 H}{g}}$

CASE 1: Projection from a height at an angle θ above horizontal:

$\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta \quad \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta$

$\mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta) \mathrm{t} \quad \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{y}}=- \mathrm{g}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{H}=(\mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2 \end{aligned}$

Case 2 : Projection from a height at an angle θ Below horizontal:

$\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta \quad \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{u} \sin \theta$

$\mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{u} \cos \theta) \mathrm{t} \quad \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{g}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{H}=(\mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{2} g \mathrm{t}^2 \\ & \mathrm{gt}^2+(2 \mathrm{u} \sin \theta) \mathrm{t}-2 \mathrm{H}=0 \end{aligned}$

Velocity after falling height h

$v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}=\sqrt{u^2+2 g h}$

Note: Four objects are projected with same speed ‘u’ from top of a tower of height ‘h’ then their speed when they reach the ground is $v=\sqrt{u^2+2 g h}$

$v \text { is independent of } \theta$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Concept of Relative Motion

Relative Displacement:

Displacement of B with respect to A = Displacement of B as measured from A

$\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{BA}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{A}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{BA}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{dt}}-\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{BA}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{A}}$

Relative = Actual – Reference

For same direction : When two particles are moving in the same direction, then magnitude of their relative velocity is equal to the difference between their individual speeds.

$\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{12}\right| \text { or }\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{21}\right|=\mathrm{v}_1 \sim \mathrm{v}_2$ ( Positive Difference )

For opposite directions : When two particles are moving in the opposite directions, then magnitude of their relative velocity is always equal to the sum of their individual speeds.

$\left|\vec{v}_{12}\right| \text { or }\left|\vec{v}_{21}\right|=v_1+v_2$

Note:- When two particles move simultaneously then the concept of relative motion becomes applicable conveniently.

Numerical Applications

(1) When two particles are moving along a straight line with constant speeds then their relative acceleration must be zero and, in this condition, relative velocity is the ratio of relative displacement to time.

$\displaystyle$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}_1=\text { const. } \quad \mathrm{v}_2=\text { const. } \\ & \text { when } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {rel. }}=0 \\ & \mathrm{v}_{\text {rel. }}=\dfrac{\mathrm{s}_{\text {Relative }}}{\text { time }} \end{aligned}$$

(2) When two particles move in such a way that their relative acceleration non-zero but constant then we apply equations of motion in the relative form.

$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{AB}} & =\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{A}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{B}} \\ & =0-\mathrm{a}=-\mathrm{a} \neq 0=\text { constant } \end{aligned}$

Equations of Motion (Relative)

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{rel}}+\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{rel}} \mathrm{t} \\ & \mathrm{~s}_{\text {rel. }}=\mathrm{u}_{\text {rel. }} \mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{a}_{\text {rel. }} \mathrm{t}^2 \\ & v_{\text {rel. }}^2=u_{\text {rel. }}^2+2 \cdot a_{\text {rel. }} s_{\text {rel. }} \\ & \mathrm{s}_{\mathrm{rel} .}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{rel} .}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel} .}\right) \mathrm{t} \end{aligned}$

Relative velocity in a plane

Relative velocity of A with respect to 'B' can be calculated as

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{v}_{A B}=\vec{v}_A-\vec{v}_B \\ & \left|\vec{v}_{A B}\right|=\sqrt{v_A^2+v_B^2-2 v_A \cdot v_B \cos \theta} \end{aligned}$

Note:

For two particles to collide:

(1) Their combined relative displacement becomes zero.

(2) Their combined vertical velocities will be same: if they are projected from same level at the same time (in case of projectiles)

(3) Their combined motion can be converted into two 1D motions.

Relative path of a projectiles w.r.t. another projectile

Two projectiles are thrown from ground with different velocities at different angles. Since both projectiles have equal accelerations so their relative acceleration is zero. Thus, path of one projectile w.r.t. other is a straight line and motion of one projectile w.r.t. other is uniform.

$\text { If } u_1 \cos \theta_1=u_2 \cos \theta_2 \text { then relative path is a vertical line. }$

$\text { If } u_1 \sin \theta_1=u_2 \sin \theta_2 \text { then relative path is a horizontal line. }$

blocks.text:
Rain-Man Concept

(1) If rain is falling vertically with a velocity $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$ and an observer is moving horizontally with speed  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}$ then the velocity of rain relative to observer will be

$\vec{v}_{R M}=\vec{v}_R-\vec{v}_M \Rightarrow \vec{v}_{R M}=-\vec{v}_R \hat{j}-\vec{v}_M \hat{i}$

$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}^2}$

The direction of  $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}$ is such that it makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical given by $\theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}} / \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}\right)$

$$(2) If rain is already falling at an angle $\theta$ with the vertical with a velocity $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$ and an observer is moving horizontally with speed $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}$ finds that the rain drops are hitting on his head vertically downwards

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Here } \vec{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}\\ &\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \sin \theta-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}\right) \mathrm{\hat i}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \cos \theta \hat{\mathrm{j}} \end{aligned}$

For rain to appear falling vertically, the horizontal component of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{RM}}$ should be zero.

{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}} \sin \theta-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}=0 \Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}}$

$\text { and }\left|\vec{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}\right|=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \cos \theta=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \sqrt{1-\sin ^2 \theta}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \sqrt{1-\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}^2}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{M}}^2}$

River-Boat (or Man) Problem

A man can swim with velocity $\vec{v}$, i.e. it is the velocity of man w.r.t. still water.

If water is also flowing with velocity $\vec{v}_R$ then velocity of man relative to ground $ \vec{v}_m=\vec{v}+\vec{v}_R$

Case(1) If the swimming is in the direction of flow of water or along the downstream then  $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}$

Case(2) If the swimming is in the direction opposite to the flow of water or along the upstream then $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}$

Case(3) If the man is crossing the river i.e. $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$ are non colinear then use vector algebra. $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{m}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}$

For shortest path :If a man wants to cross the river such that his "displacement should be minimum".

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{m}}=\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{R}}\right)$It is in the direction of displacement AB.

$\text { To reach at } B $,  $\mathrm v \sin \theta=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mathrm{v}}$

$\text { Time taken } \mathrm{T}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{v} \cos \theta}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{v}^2-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}^2}}$

For minimum time:  To cross the river in minimum time, the velocity along AB $(v \cos \theta)$ should be maximum.

It is possible if $\theta=0$  i.e. swimming should start perpendicular to water current.

$\text { Minimum time }=\mathrm{t}_{\min }=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{v}}$

In time $\mathrm{t}_{\text {min }}$swimmer travels distance  BC along the river with speed of river  $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{R}} \therefore \mathrm{BC}=\mathbf{t}_{\min } \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{R}}$

$\text { Distance travelled along river flow }=\text { drift of } \operatorname{man}=t_{\min } v_R=\dfrac{d}{V} v_R$
